claims.text: Stripe Minions produce over 1,300 merged pull requests per week as of February 2026, up from 1,000+ at first disclosure, with humans reviewing the code but writing none of it.
InfoQ reports Stripe engineers said Minions now produce over 1,300 pull requests per week, up from 1,000 in earlier trials, and all changes are human-reviewed but contain no human-written code.
Minions run on pre-warmed 'devboxes', standardized AWS EC2 instances that provision in about 10 seconds.
Minion devboxes are identical to the environments human engineers use, but are isolated from production and the internet (no production access, no internet).

Stripe's devboxes are cloud machines pre-loaded with the entire codebase, tools, and services; they spin up in ten seconds because Stripe proactively provisions and warms a pool of them, cloning repositories, warming caches, and starting background services ahead of time.
Engineers already used one devbox per task, and a single engineer might have half a dozen running at once; agents slot into this same pattern.

An unattended agent needs isolation (mistakes can't touch production), parallelism (multiple agents on separate tasks), and predictability (every agent starts from a clean, consistent state), and Stripe's devboxes already provided all three.
Stripe describes Minion devboxes as 'cattle, not pets': ephemeral, reproducible, disposable environments, so the agent gets a clean environment every time and accumulates no state from prior runs.

Per a video walkthrough, because each devbox is sandboxed with no internet or production access, no human permission checks are needed; the isolation acts as the permission, and independent devboxes allow parallelization without git worktree conflicts.

A video walkthrough says Stripe found that git worktrees and containers on a developer's laptop make permissioning hard to get right at scale, so every Minion run uses an isolated cloud AWS EC2 instance.
A blueprint is a sequence of nodes where some nodes run deterministic code and others run an agentic loop, alternating rigid and creative steps.
In blueprints, the 'implement the feature' and 'fix CI failures' steps get the full agentic loop with tools and freedom, while 'run linters' and 'push the branch' steps are hardcoded.
In the described pipeline, the agent writes code, a hardcoded step always runs the linter, the agent fixes lint issues, then a hardcoded git commit occurs and the agent continues.

Blueprints are workflows defined in code that specify how a task is divided into subtasks handled either by deterministic routines or by the agent; Stripe engineers describe them as agent skills interwoven with code.
Minions are built on a fork of Block's open-source Goose agent, tailored for unattended runs, with a Toolshed MCP server providing nearly 500 internal tools.
The CI strategy is local lint (under 5 seconds), at most 2 CI rounds, and auto-applied fixes, after which the result goes to a human even if failures remain.

After an implementation step the harness does not ask the model to judge correctness; it runs a selected subset of Stripe's more than 3 million tests, feeds failure output back to the agent, and produces a pull request if tests pass within at most two CI rounds.

Reliability is reinforced through CI/CD pipelines, automated tests, and static analysis before human review, and engineers noted Minions perform best on well-defined tasks such as configuration adjustments, dependency upgrades, and minor refactoring.
Minions do not merge; the agents write code and open the pull request, and humans must still review everything, which is flagged as a potential human review bottleneck.
Minions can be invoked via Slack (the primary interface), CLI, web UI, or internal tool integrations.
One documented trigger is a Slack emoji reaction on a message describing the desired change, which starts a run without an engineer monitoring it.
The code managed by Minions supports more than $1 trillion in annual payment volume at Stripe, per InfoQ.
Stripe has not published example PRs, so outsiders cannot judge whether the 1,300/week figure represents substantive changes or low-stakes mechanical work.

One secondary source claims about 70% of Minions' roughly 1,300 weekly PRs were merged without any human modification, and dates the disclosure to early 2025, which conflicts with the February 2026 dating in other sources.
